prompt: Priya says: "Can we build alerts for saved searches?" Which is the strongest first move?

options.text: Start writing the check-job code for the most obvious version — immediate email alerts — since that's what "alerts" almost always means
List the individual decisions buried in the request (frequency, duplicate handling, unsubscribe, scope) and sort each into "Priya's call" or "my call" before writing anything
Ask Priya to write the full technical spec herself, since she knows the product and its users best

hints: "Alerts for saved searches" isn't one decision — it's several, bundled into one sentence.
The goal isn't to guess the obvious version fast; it's to know which of the buried decisions you're even allowed to guess at.
explanation: Decomposing the request before building anything is what separates a spec from a guess dressed up as one. Jumping straight to the "obvious" immediate-alerts version skips the step where you'd have discovered that frequency is actually Priya's call, not an assumption to bake in — you might get lucky and guess right, or you might ship exactly the spam problem this domain's own worked example warns about. Handing the whole spec to Priya goes wrong in the other direction: she has no useful opinion on duplicate-prevention or email escaping, and asking her to develop one wastes her time on a job that's yours.

prompt: Which of these is a decision that's Priya's to make, not yours?

options.text: Whether alert emails go out immediately per match or get batched into a daily digest
Whether the check job tracks "already alerted" state as a stored timestamp or a set of listing IDs
Which email-templating approach escapes user-supplied content safely by default

hints: Ask: does this change what a user or the business experiences, or only how the code gets there?
One of these three has a real product-and-reputation tradeoff behind it. The other two are implementation details with no visible effect if done well.
explanation: Immediate-versus-digest changes what users actually experience and how RemoteCraft's sends look to a mail provider watching for spam — a business tradeoff Priya is accountable for, not a technical detail. The other two options have zero visible effect on the product as long as they work: whether duplicates are tracked by timestamp or ID, and which escaping approach is used, are exactly the kind of decisions that belong to the developer, and bringing either one to Priya would waste a meeting on a question she has no useful opinion about.

prompt: v1 is scoped: immediate alerts only, no digest mode, no SMS. A teammate suggests quietly building digest mode too, "since it's not much extra work, might as well." What's the strongest reason not to?

options.text: An addition made outside the written brief isn't reviewed, isn't dated, and isn't something anyone actually agreed to — if it causes a problem, there's no record of the decision to point back to
Digest mode is technically harder to implement correctly than immediate alerts, so it should always wait regardless of how much spare time exists
Priya explicitly forbade building digest mode, so adding it now would be dishonest

hints: The brief didn't say "don't build digest mode" — it said v1 doesn't include it. Those aren't the same thing.
Think about what the decision log habit from this domain is actually protecting against.
explanation: The brief's explicit scope cuts are what let a decision log actually be trusted later — every item in it was reviewed and agreed to at a specific point. Quietly building extra scope "since it's not much work" routes around that: it's an undocumented decision made by whoever happened to have spare time, which is exactly the failure mode this domain has been warning about since lesson one. "Technically harder" isn't the actual reason to hold off — a genuinely easy addition built outside the agreed scope is still an undocumented decision, just a cheap one. And Priya didn't forbid digest mode; she deferred it. Treating a deferral as a prohibition mischaracterizes what actually happened and isn't the real objection here.

prompt: You're two hours into building the alerts feature. Which moment is the right time to write a decision-log entry?

options.text: The moment the decision is actually made, in one line — what was decided, why, and what wasn't done instead
At the end of the day, reconstructing the day's choices from memory in a short summary paragraph
Only once the code has shipped and worked in production for a week, to make sure the decision turned out to matter

hints: Reasoning reconstructed after the fact tends to sound more certain than it actually was in the moment.
You can't know in advance which decisions will turn out to matter.
explanation: Writing the entry at decision time captures the real uncertainty you had then — including a guess that felt like a guess, not a choice that felt inevitable in hindsight. Waiting until end-of-day loses exactly that: memory smooths reasoning into something more confident and more linear than it actually was, which is less defensible later, not more. Waiting for production outcomes fails differently — you can't tell in advance which routine-looking decision (like a checkpoint timestamp) will turn into a real bug and which won't, so filtering by "turned out to matter" means most of the log never gets written at all.

prompt: In the worked exemplar, `checkSavedSearch` queries listings with `createdAt: { gt: search.lastCheckedAt }` and then sets `lastCheckedAt: new Date()` after all the alert emails have been sent. What's the actual fix?

options.text: Capture the query's start time before running it, and checkpoint to that captured time instead of the time when processing finished
Change gt to gte so nothing created exactly at the checkpoint boundary is ever excluded
Wrap the whole function in a database transaction so the query and the update happen atomically

hints: The bug isn't about which listings satisfy the comparison — it's about which moment in time gets written back as the checkpoint.
Think about what happens to a listing created during the gap between the query running and the update finishing.
explanation: The gap exists because the checkpoint is stamped with the time processing *finished*, which is later than the time the query actually ran — anything created in between is invisible to both this run (query already executed) and every future run (checkpoint has already moved past it). Capturing `queryStartedAt` before the query runs and checkpointing to that value closes the gap: anything created after the query started is now guaranteed to appear in the *next* run's results, because the checkpoint never advances past a moment the query didn't actually cover. Switching gt to gte doesn't touch this — the boundary the comparison operator controls was never the problem, and gte here would actually reintroduce duplicates on any run that finds nothing new. A transaction wrapping the query and update wouldn't help either: the emails are sent between the two, outside any transaction's atomicity, and the gap is about wall-clock timing during that send, not about the query and update racing each other.

prompt:
The alert email template builds its body with `` `

New match: ${listing.title}

` ``. Why is escaping `listing.title` before interpolating it the right fix, rather than just rejecting listing titles that contain `<` or `>`?

options.text: Escaping keeps every legitimate title, including ones with real angle brackets in the role name, displaying correctly, while still preventing any of it from being parsed as markup
Rejecting titles with those characters would be slower to run than escaping them, since validation adds an extra pass over the string
It doesn't matter which approach is used, as long as the fix happens somewhere before the email is sent

hints: A job titled "Engineer <Level II>" is a legitimate title, not an attack — what should happen to it?
Rejecting valid input is its own kind of bug, even when the rejection is aimed at the right root cause.
explanation: Escaping fixes the actual channel problem — user content is separated from markup syntax — without losing any legitimate data. A real listing titled with angle brackets in it still displays exactly as written; it just can't be misread as an HTML tag. Rejecting titles containing `<` or `>` outright would turn a formatting problem into a data-loss problem, silently blocking legitimate listings for a reason that has nothing to do with the job itself. Speed isn't the deciding factor here — both approaches are cheap — and "it doesn't matter which" ignores that one of the two options breaks valid input while the other doesn't.

prompt: Jordan asks: "How much of this did you actually build?" Which opening best sets up the rest of a defensible answer?

options.text: "I used an AI tool to draft the mechanical parts — the matcher query, the email boilerplate — and made the product and judgment calls myself. I can walk you through both, and where the AI got something wrong."
"Most of it, honestly — I only used AI for small bits here and there."
"It's a pretty standard AI-assisted build, nothing unusual about the process."

hints: The strongest opening is the one that promises something specific and checkable is coming next.
Vague reassurance ("nothing unusual," "only small bits") answers a different, easier question than the one being asked.
explanation: This opening does two things at once: it states the actual delegation split honestly, and it signals that a concrete follow-up is available, which is what makes the rest of the conversation go well. "Only used AI for small bits" is vague enough to mean almost anything, and if the codebase later shows an AI-drafted first commit for the whole matcher, the mismatch reads worse than an honest "I delegated the mechanical parts" would have from the start. "Nothing unusual about the process" answers a question about typicality, not about this specific feature — it's the kind of non-answer that invites a sharper follow-up rather than closing the topic.

prompt: Which of these is the strongest thing to say when asked what you refused to delegate to the AI tool?

options.text: "Whether alerts are gated behind a paywall, and the checkpoint-timing fix — both required weighing something the tool has no way to check against: business tradeoffs, and reasoning about a race condition under real timing, not a pattern in training data."
"I generally prefer to stay hands-on with as much of the code as possible."
"I don't fully trust AI tools, so I double-check everything regardless of how routine it is."

hints: "Refused to delegate" is strongest when it names a specific decision and the specific reason the tool couldn't have made it — not a general stance.
"I double-check everything" describes a review habit, not a decision that was withheld from delegation in the first place.
explanation: Naming the paywall decision and the checkpoint-timing fix, with the specific reason each one required judgment the tool doesn't have access to, is exactly the kind of claim that survives a follow-up question — it points at something real and checkable in the decision log. "I prefer to stay hands-on" is a working style, not a reasoned boundary, and doesn't explain why any particular decision needed to stay with you. "I don't fully trust AI tools" describes blanket suspicion rather than a considered split between what's safe to delegate and what isn't — and it actually undercuts the earlier part of the defense, where mechanical work genuinely was delegated with good reason.

prompt: Which bug story is the strongest thing to lead with when Jordan asks "where did the AI get something wrong"?

options.text: "The checkpoint was stamped with the time processing finished, not when the query ran — a listing created in that gap would've been silently missed forever. I traced it by hand, then fixed it by capturing the query's start time instead."
"AI-generated code sometimes has subtle bugs, so I always review it closely before shipping."
"It occasionally suggests outdated syntax, which I catch and correct as I go."

hints: The strongest version names the actual bug, the actual mechanism, and the actual fix — not a general habit.
"I always review closely" is true of every good candidate and demonstrates nothing about this specific feature.
explanation: This version is checkable: it names the specific defect, explains the mechanism (the gap between query time and checkpoint time), and states the fix — exactly the kind of claim a hiring manager can probe further and get a real answer to. "I always review closely" is a generic statement that could be said about any feature with no work behind it, and proves nothing about whether real judgment was exercised here. "Outdated syntax" describes a much shallower category of error — a style or version mismatch — not the kind of judgment-requiring bug this capstone's rubric is actually built around, and leading with it undersells the harder catch that's actually available to tell.

prompt: Which repository history makes the strongest portfolio artefact for this feature?

options.text: Separate, reviewable commits: the AI-drafted matcher, the checkpoint-timing fix, and the escaping fix each as their own commit with a message explaining the change
A single squashed commit titled "add alerts feature" that includes the finished, working code
The finished code with no commit history at all, plus a polished README describing the process

hints: An artefact is supposed to be checkable — think about what a reviewer would actually want to open and compare against the decision log.
A README describing a process is a claim. A commit history showing that process is evidence.
explanation: Separate commits let a reviewer open the checkpoint-timing fix and the escaping fix independently, and check each one against the corresponding decision-log entry and review note — which is the entire point of an artefact-first portfolio: it can be verified, not just read. A single squashed commit hides exactly where the judgment happened, forcing a reviewer to take the README's word for it. No history at all is worse still — however polished the README, there's nothing underneath it to check the claims against, which defeats the purpose of leading with an artefact instead of a résumé line.

prompt: Which estimate for the next feature is the most sustainable one to give a client or manager?

options.text: "Three days on a normal week, up to six on a bad one — if it's a bad week, the first thing I'd cut is the digest-mode groundwork, not the core alert flow."
"Five days" — a single number quietly padded to absorb an unpredictable week, without saying so
"Three days" — the estimate for a normal week, stated as the commitment regardless of how the week actually goes

hints: A range that names its own floor communicates something a padded single number doesn't.
Naming what gets cut on a bad week, in advance, is the same skill as the explicit scope-cutting from the first lesson in this domain — applied to your own capacity instead of a feature's scope.
explanation: The range with a named floor and a named cut gives the other person something to actually plan around: a worst case, and what happens if it's hit. A quietly padded single number looks more certain than it is — if the week goes normally, the padding just reads as slow delivery, and if it goes badly, there's no stated plan for what happens to scope, only a missed date. A flat "three days" stated as a hard commitment regardless of capacity is the least sustainable of the three: it treats a good-week estimate as a promise, with nothing built in for the week that doesn't go that way.

prompt: Which availability statement to a new client is the most practical and trust-building?

options.text: "Written status by end of day, most days. Calls scheduled with at least 48 hours' notice. If a project needs to pause for a stretch, I'll flag it as soon as I know, along with what it does to the timeline."
A statement that includes a specific diagnosis and a description of how symptoms vary day to day
"I'll always be available when you need me — don't worry about it."

hints: The strongest version is made of commitments the other person can hold you to, not information they didn't ask for.
A promise that can't actually be kept is riskier than a named contingency, not safer.
explanation: This version gives a client three concrete things to plan around — an update cadence, a scheduling norm, and a named contingency for a bad stretch — none of which require them to know anything about why. A specific diagnosis isn't the client's business and doesn't build trust the way a concrete commitment does; it tends to make the other person unsure how to respond, which works against the goal. "I'll always be available" is a promise that will eventually be broken by an ordinary bad week, and breaking it with no contingency named in advance costs more trust than stating the honest, practical version up front ever would.

prompt: A vague product ask has been turned into a scoped brief with explicit v1 cuts. Which practice best protects that scoping from quietly eroding over the course of the build?

options.text: Treating any addition outside the written brief as its own decision that needs a one-line log entry and, if it's non-trivial, a conversation with the product owner before it's built
Trusting that the team will remember the original scope, since it was discussed once at the start of the sprint
Re-reviewing the entire brief line by line every morning before starting work
Letting whichever engineer is fastest that day decide what additional scope is reasonable to include

explanation: Scope erodes in small, individually reasonable-looking additions, not in one obvious violation — which is exactly why each addition needs to be treated as its own decision, logged and reviewed like any other, rather than assumed to be fine because it's small. Relying on memory is how "might as well, it's not much extra" additions slip in unlogged. A full daily re-review is expensive enough that it won't survive a bad week and doesn't scale as a habit. Letting the fastest engineer decide reintroduces the exact problem this domain opened with: a decision that affects the product, made silently by whoever happened to be typing.

prompt: An AI tool is asked to write a job that processes records newer than a stored checkpoint, then advances that checkpoint. What question should the spec answer explicitly to avoid the class of bug in this domain's worked exemplar?

options.text: Exactly which moment in time the checkpoint should be set to — the moment the query ran, not the moment processing of the results finished
Whether the language's date-comparison operator uses strict or loose equality
Whether the checkpoint should be stored as a Unix timestamp or an ISO 8601 string

explanation: The exemplar's bug wasn't about equality semantics or storage format — it was about which real-world instant got written back as "now." Any record created between the query running and the checkpoint being written falls into a permanent gap unless the spec is explicit that the checkpoint reflects query time, not completion time. Equality strictness is a real but unrelated concern for the comparison itself, and storage format is a serialization detail with no bearing on which moment gets captured.

prompt: A decision log entry reads: "Used a stored timestamp for duplicate prevention." What's missing that would make this entry actually useful at a defense three months later?

options.text: The alternative that was considered and rejected, and the specific reason it lost out
The exact line number in the file where the timestamp is stored
A restatement of what a timestamp is, for anyone reading the log who isn't a developer

explanation: As written, this entry sounds like the only option that ever existed — it doesn't show that any judgment was exercised. Adding the rejected alternative (e.g. "rather than a set of alerted listing IDs, which would need cleanup logic this feature doesn't otherwise require") is what turns a bare statement into evidence of a considered decision, which is exactly what a defense conversation asks about. A line number goes stale the moment the file changes and belongs in the code, not the log. Explaining what a timestamp is wastes the log's brevity on something any technical reader already knows — the log's job is the reasoning, not a glossary.

prompt: A candidate's portfolio README says only "AI-assisted" with no further detail, on a repository with no decision log or review notes. What's the strongest reason this weakens the portfolio piece, rather than merely being brief?

options.text: It asks to be taken on faith, which defeats the purpose of an artefact-first portfolio — there's nothing next to the claim that a reviewer could actually check it against
It's technically inaccurate, since no feature is ever purely AI-generated
It uses a term ("AI-assisted") that carries negative connotations and should be avoided entirely in a portfolio

explanation: The whole value of an artefact-first portfolio is that claims can be verified against evidence sitting right next to them — a decision log, review notes, a commit history. "AI-assisted" with nothing backing it up is just a claim, indistinguishable from one that's overclaiming or hiding something, because there's no way to check it. The term itself isn't the problem, and avoiding it wouldn't fix anything — the fix is supplying the evidence the claim needs to be credible, not rewording the claim.

prompt: During a client conversation, someone asks, bluntly, "so did you even write any of this?" about a feature that was genuinely AI-drafted and then reviewed, fixed, and shipped by you. Which response best holds up?

options.text: Naming specifically what was delegated, what you decided and fixed, and one concrete bug you caught — rather than a defensive yes/no answer to the literal question
A firm "yes, I wrote all of it," to avoid the conversation turning into a debate about AI tools
"Does it matter, as long as it works?" — redirecting the question toward the outcome rather than the process

explanation: The blunt question is really asking whether real judgment was exercised, and the specific, checkable answer — what was delegated, what was decided, what bug was caught and how — answers that directly, whether or not it matches the literal wording of the question. Claiming sole authorship when that's not true is a specific, discoverable falsehood the moment anyone looks at the process. "Does it matter" dodges a legitimate question about process and judgment, and in a client relationship built on trust, dodging tends to read as having something to hide — even when nothing was actually hidden.

prompt: A graduate is preparing an estimate for a new client and wants it to survive a bad week without either overpromising or oversharing. Which approach fits?

options.text: A stated range with a named floor and a pre-identified cut for the low end, communicated as a normal part of scoping the work
A single confident number, with a private mental buffer the client is never told about
A detailed explanation of the health condition that causes capacity to vary, offered upfront so the client understands the range

explanation: A stated range with a named floor and a specific, pre-identified cut gives the client something concrete to plan around, and it's honest about the variable without requiring any private information to justify it. A single number with a hidden buffer isn't actually safer — it just moves the honesty problem to the delivery date, where it shows up as either an unexplained delay or wasted slack nobody knew was there. Offering health details isn't necessary to make the range credible — the working commitments (the range itself, the named cut) do that job on their own, and the estimate should be built to work whether or not the reason behind it is ever mentioned.

prompt: Priya has said "can we build alerts for saved searches?" and nothing more. List at least four specific sub-decisions buried in that request, sort each one into "Priya's call" or "your call," and for each of Priya's-call items, write the actual question you'd bring to her along with a recommended default she can just approve or override.
hints: Think through the whole lifecycle: when a search gets saved, when a check runs, when an email gets sent, and what happens when a user wants it to stop.
For Priya's-call items, don't just ask an open question — bringing a recommended default is what makes the conversation five minutes instead of thirty.
At least one of your four decisions should be a pure implementation detail with no product-visible effect, to show you can tell the two kinds apart.
explanation: A strong answer names decisions across the lifecycle and sorts them correctly, for example: (1) **Alert frequency** — immediate vs digest — Priya's call; question: "Immediate per match, or a daily digest? I'd lean immediate, since we're small enough that a slow digest risks users hearing about a good match from a competitor's alert first — but this affects our send volume and reputation, so it's your call." (2) **Feature access** — free for all users, or paywalled — Priya's call; question: "Should saved-search alerts be free for everyone, or a paid-tier feature? No strong recommendation from me — this is a monetization call." (3) **Duplicate prevention mechanism** (stored checkpoint vs a set of alerted IDs) — your call, no question needed for Priya. (4) **Email escaping approach** for user-generated listing content — your call, no question needed. A weak answer either treats every decision as needing Priya's input (wasting her time on implementation detail) or silently assumes an answer to a genuinely product-shaped question like alert frequency, which is exactly the failure this lesson opened with.

prompt: Write the scoped-brief section of your spec for the alerts feature: what v1 does, and — as its own explicit list — what is deferred to v2 and why each item was cut rather than included. Include at least three deferred items, each with a one-sentence justification that isn't just "no time."
hints: A justification like "no time" isn't a real reason — it's true of almost anything you could ever cut. Say what makes this specific item safe to defer.
Good candidates to consider: digest mode, SMS/push notifications, an admin dashboard for alert volume, per-search snooze, retry-with-backoff on delivery failure.
The explicit-cuts list is itself part of the deliverable — it's what stops scope creep from happening silently later.
explanation: A strong answer states v1 clearly (saved searches trigger immediate per-match email alerts, with a working unsubscribe link) and then lists deferrals with real justification, for example: "Digest mode — deferred, because it requires a second delivery path and a preference UI neither of which block the core value of getting alerted at all"; "SMS/push — deferred, because it needs a new delivery integration RemoteCraft doesn't have yet, and email covers the actual user complaint that prompted this feature"; "Admin dashboard for alert volume — deferred, because nobody has asked for it yet and building observability before the feature has real usage data is premature." A weak answer either omits the reasoning ("digest mode — v2") or gives a reason that would apply to literally anything ("not enough time"), which fails to demonstrate that the cut was a considered decision rather than an arbitrary one.

prompt: Write the decision-log entry for the checkpoint-timing fix from this lesson's worked exemplar. It must include: what was decided, why, and the alternative (the AI tool's original approach) that was rejected — in roughly one to three sentences, in the style this lesson describes as worth keeping for a defense.
hints: State the fix as a decision, not as a bug report — the log is about what you chose to do, not a narrative of discovering the problem.
Name the rejected alternative specifically: what would have happened if the original AI-generated checkpoint logic had shipped as-is?
Keep it to a sentence or two — a decision log entry that's too long to skim in five seconds stops being useful in a defense.
explanation: A strong entry: "Checkpoint `lastCheckedAt` to the query's start time, not the time processing finishes. The AI-generated version stamped it with `new Date()` after all emails were sent — any listing created during that send window would fall into a gap no future run's query would ever cover, silently dropping real matches forever." This names the decision, the reason, and the rejected alternative in two sentences, and it's specific enough that a reader could go find the corresponding commit and verify the claim. A weak entry either omits the alternative ("fixed the checkpoint timing bug" — fixed how, and compared to what?) or is too vague to be checkable ("improved the reliability of the check job").

prompt: The AI-generated `sendAlertEmail` function built its HTML body by interpolating `listing.title` and `listing.company` directly into a template literal. Write the fixed version's approach (in words or pseudocode — you don't need working code), and describe the specific test input you'd use to verify the fix actually closes the gap, plus what the test should assert.
hints: The fix needs to escape the characters that have special meaning in HTML before they're interpolated: <, >, &, and ".

A good verification input should contain at least one of those characters in a position that would previously have broken rendering — reuse the listing title from this lesson's diagnose-mechanism section if it helps.
The assertion should check that the dangerous characters appear in the output as their escaped form, not that the email 'looks right' by eye.
explanation: A strong answer: escape `<`, `>`, `&`, and `"` in any user-supplied field (title, company) before interpolating it into the HTML string — either with a small hand-written escaping function or a templating library that escapes by default — so `<Remote, EU-only>` becomes `<Remote, EU-only>` and displays as literal text. Verification: build an alert email for a listing titled `Senior Engineer <Remote, EU-only>` and assert that the resulting HTML string contains the literal substring `<Remote, EU-only>` rather than an unescaped `<Remote, EU-only>` — the same input from the lesson's diagnose-mechanism section that originally exposed the bug is exactly the right regression-test input, because it reproduces the failure deterministically. A weak answer describes only "sanitizing the input" without naming which characters matter or why, or proposes a test that merely checks the email "renders" without asserting on the actual escaped content, which wouldn't have caught the original bug in the first place.

prompt: Write your own 90-second defense answer to "walk me through this feature" for the RemoteCraft alerts feature, following the three-part structure from this lesson: what you delegated and why it was safe, what you refused to delegate and why, and one concrete story of where the AI was wrong and how you caught it. You must use the checkpoint-timing bug as your concrete story, told with the specific mechanism (query time vs. completion time), not just "there was a bug."
hints: Aim for roughly four to six sentences — long enough to be specific, short enough to actually take 90 seconds spoken aloud.
The delegated part should name specific pieces (the matcher, the email boilerplate), not just say "some of the code."
The refused part should name the actual reason a human judgment call was needed — not a general statement about caution.
explanation: A strong answer, in structure: "This is a saved-search alerts feature for RemoteCraft — when a listing matches a search a user's turned alerts on for, they get an email. I used an AI tool to draft the mechanical parts: the database query that matches new listings against a saved search's filters, and the email template boilerplate. I made the call on alert frequency myself — immediate per match rather than a digest — because that's a product tradeoff around user experience and spam risk that needed the product owner's input, not the AI's guess. In review, I caught a real bug: the AI's version checkpointed the 'last checked' time using the wall-clock moment processing finished, not when the query actually ran — so a listing created while emails were still being sent would fall into a permanent gap no later run would ever catch. I fixed it by capturing the query's start time and checkpointing to that instead, and added a regression test for it." A weak answer either skips the mechanism of the bug ("there was a timing bug I fixed") or omits one of the three required parts entirely, which is exactly the gap a good interviewer's follow-up question would expose.

prompt: Priya, reviewing the finished feature, asks bluntly: "So did you even write any of this, or did the AI do it all?" Write your response. It must avoid both extremes covered in this lesson — claiming sole authorship of AI-drafted code, and describing your own review and judgment as merely "approving" what the AI produced.
hints: The honest answer is specific about both what the tool did and what you did — neither erased.
Naming one real thing you decided or caught is worth more here than a general statement about your process.
Consider ending with an offer to walk through the specifics — that's what makes an answer like this credible rather than defensive.
explanation: A strong response: "An AI tool drafted the first version of the matcher query and the email template — that part's true. But the alert-frequency call was mine, made with your input specifically because it's a product tradeoff. And the feature almost shipped with a bug where a listing created during the alert run would've been silently missed forever — I caught that in review, traced why it happened, and fixed it. So it's closer to: the AI wrote a first draft of the mechanical parts, and the decisions and the catches were mine. Happy to walk through the specific commit if that's useful." This names the true parts of both claims — AI did draft real code, and real judgment was exercised — without collapsing into either "I wrote it all" or "the AI wrote it, I just approved it." A weak answer picks one side defensively (over-asserting personal authorship, or self-effacingly minimizing the review work that actually mattered) rather than giving the specific, checkable middle version that's actually true.

prompt: Write your own availability-and-estimating paragraph for a prospective client or employer, to be used alongside a portfolio piece like the RemoteCraft alerts feature. It must include: a concrete update cadence, how meetings get scheduled and why, a named contingency for a low-capacity stretch, and a range estimate (with a stated floor) for a feature roughly the size of the alerts feature. It must not include any medical or diagnostic detail, and must not promise availability will never vary.
hints: Treat this as something you'd actually send to a client before a project starts, not an internal note to yourself.
The named contingency should say what happens to the timeline, specifically — not just that you'll 'let them know.'
The estimate should look like the range-with-a-named-cut pattern from this lesson, not a padded single number.
explanation: A strong paragraph names all four required elements concretely, for example: "I work async-first: expect a written status update by end of day, most days, rather than real-time availability. Calls are scheduled with at least 48 hours' notice, since a synchronous conversation costs more focus than an async update and I plan around that. If capacity drops for a stretch, I'll flag it as soon as I know, along with what it does to the timeline — typically, cutting whatever's lowest-priority in the current scope before touching the delivery date on the core work. For a feature around the size of a saved-search-alerts build, I'd estimate three days on a normal week, up to six on a harder one — if it's a harder week, the first thing I'd cut is any polish beyond the core flow, not the flow itself." A weak answer either includes unnecessary personal or medical detail (undermining the practical, competent framing this lesson argues for), promises availability that can't realistically be guaranteed, or gives a single point estimate with no stated floor or named contingency, which fails the exact test this lesson sets up.
